title: this, and Why Arrows Differ
summary: How this is decided by the call, and why arrow functions borrow it.

steps.title: this is decided by the call
body: In C#, `this` is always the object the method belongs to. In JavaScript, for ordinary functions and methods, `this` is decided by **how the function is called**:
t.show();               // "tea": called as t.show(), so this = t

`obj.method()` sets `this` to `obj`. Pull the method off the object and call it bare, and `this` is lost. That happens every time you pass a method as a callback: `button.addEventListener("click", t.show)`, `setTimeout(t.show, 10)`, `items.map(t.format)`.

code: try { f(); } catch (e) { console.log("error:", (e as Error).constructor.name); }
steps.explain: Called bare, `f` has no object, so `this` is `undefined` and reading `this.name` throws a `TypeError`. (`as Error` is a TypeScript cast that Node strips.)

steps.title: Arrow functions borrow this
body: An arrow function has **no `this` of its own**. It uses the `this` of the place it was written, exactly like a captured variable. So arrows are the fix for callbacks:
// an arrow stored as a field: `this` is always this instance
The other fixes are `t.show.bind(t)` (makes a copy with `this` fixed) or wrapping: `() => t.show()`.
The flip side: **do not** use an arrow when you want `this` to be the calling object, such as a method defined in an object literal.

steps.prompt: Does `this` inside the function depend on how it is called?

steps.explain: The arrow field is bound to `c` forever. The method is called through a wrapper `() => c.incMethod()`, so it is still called on `c`.

steps.prompt: A callback `this.items.map(function (x) { return x * this.factor; })` inside a class method fails. What is the simplest modern fix?
options: Wrap the class in a closure
steps.explain: The arrow uses the method's `this`. (`const self = this` was the pre-2015 workaround.)

steps.title: A counter object
prompt: Write `makeStepper(step: number)` returning an object literal `{ value, next() }`:
- `next()` adds `step` to `this.value` and returns the object itself, so calls can chain
Use a **method** (not an arrow) for `next`, because it must use the object's own `this`.
template: Dojo.eq("value kept on the object", 10, dojoS.value);
hints: Method syntax inside an object literal: `next() { ... }`.
